records.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in structured reasoning and symbolic tasks, with coding emerging as a particularly successful application. Yet, despite apparent parallels between programming and proof construction, advances in formalized mathematics have proven significantly more challenging. records.title: Unsafer in Many Turns: Benchmarking and Defending Multi-Turn Safety Risks in Tool-Using Agents
records.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable, yet their safety lags behind. This creates a gap between what agents can do and should do. This gap widens as agents engage in multi-turn interactions and employ diverse tools, introducing new risks overlooked by existing benchmarks. To systematically scale safety testing into multi-turn, tool-realistic settings, we propose a principled taxonomy that transforms single-turn harmful tasks into multi-turn attack sequences. Using this taxonomy, we construct MT-AgentRisk (Multi-Turn Agent Risk Benchmark), the first benchmark to evaluate multi-turn tool-using agent safety. Our experiments reveal substantial safety degradation: the Attack Success Rate (ASR) increases by 16% on average across open and closed models in multi-turn settings. To close this gap, we propose ToolShield, a training-free, tool-agnostic, self-exploration defense: when encountering a new tool, the agent autonomously generates test cases, executes them to observe downstream effects, and distills safety experiences for deployment. Experiments show that ToolShield effectively reduces ASR by 30% on average in multi-turn interactions. Our code is available at https://github.com/CHATS-lab/ToolShield.

records.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model prompts are widely treated as portable text, yet research demonstrates that formatting alone causes accuracy variations of up to 78.3 percentage points within a single model and optimal format overlap between model families falls below an Intersection-over-Union of 0.2. We argue that existing terminology -- model drifting, prompt brittleness, prompt sensitivity -- describes symptoms of a deeper structural phenomenon we term prompt coupling: the degree of interdependence between a prompt and the specific LLM it targets. records.title: EduRobust: Multilingual Robustness of System Prompt Restrictions in Educational LLM Deployments
records.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in educational platforms through instructable behavioral guardrails encoded as system prompts (e.g., "do not solve homework problems for students''). However, safety alignment in modern LLMs is predominantly English-centric, leaving their behavior in other languages underexplored. We present a two-phase study using EduRobust, a reproducible benchmarking framework for multilingual system prompt robustness. In Phase 1 we measure the vulnerability gap: 5 educational behavioral restrictions are tested across 24 languages, 3 open-source LLMs, and 50 repeated trials per configuration (18,000 cells). In Phase 2 we test three candidate defenses: (A) strategy-aware prompt hardening, (B) multilingual system prompts, and (C) composite English-only anchoring. The inverted resource-tier gradient persists under all three defenses, and multilingual model capability proves to be a double-edged sword --- amplifying both attack susceptibility and defense responsiveness. We release the full framework; including attack templates, translation cache, defense variants, evaluation harness, and analysis scripts; to support reproducible multilingual safety research in the educational AI community.

records.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) are transforming modern transportation by integrating advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), sensor technologies, and real-time decision-making systems. However, ensuring safety and reliability in such systems remains a critical challenge due to their operation in dynamic and uncertain environments. This chapter presents a comprehensive analysis of safety challenges in autonomous driving, focusing on safety-critical system behavior, diverse sources of risks, and complex edge-case scenarios. It further explores reliability frameworks tailored for agentic AV systems, emphasizing fault tolerance, redundancy, and distributed multi-agent architectures that enhance robustness and scalability. Additionally, the chapter discusses advanced safety assurance mechanisms, including formal verification, runtime safety monitoring, explainable AI, and ethical decision-making frameworks. By integrating these approaches, the chapter highlights how intelligent, transparent, and resilient AV systems can be developed to meet stringent safety requirements.</jats:p>

records.title: The Risks of Agentic AI in Autonomous Vehicles
records.abstract: <jats:p>The agentic artificial intelligence is quickly changing the abilities of autonomous cars, allowing them to decide more autonomously and goal-oriented. Although this development is an efficiency and a mobility game changer, it brings along novel safety, control, and ethical dimensions. In this chapter the author discusses the exceptional risks introduced by agentic AI in a self-driving system, such as perception and planning errors, loss of human control, unstable emergent behaviors within the system, as well as the problem of offering machine decisions that reflect the societal values. It emphasizes regulatory shortcomings in existing regulations, discusses the possible areas of liability, and considers recent mitigation measures like effective control systems, transparency, and AI design that are value-oriented. Finally, the chapter also offers a detailed discussion of the role of agentic autonomy in risk in Alexrondi and Fleischer transportation and suggests ways of creating safer and ethically responsible autonomous vehicles systems.</jats:p>

records.title: Autonomous Governance of Agentic Financial Systems: A Multi-Agent Regulatory Framework for Real-Time Market Integrity Surveillance and Systemic Risk Mitigation
records.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid deployment of Agentic AI systems in financial markets has outpaced existing governance frameworks, creating unprecedented systemic risks from emergent behaviors such as algorithmic collusion, spoofing, and cascading market destabilization. This paper proposes and implements an Auto-Regulatory Agentic Framework (ARAF) comprising specialized AI agents that autonomously monitor trading behavior, detect emergent anomalies, and execute real-time regulatory interventions. Using a simulated multi-agent market environment with heterogeneous trading strategies (normal, spoofing, collusive), we demonstrate that our framework achieves a detection rate of 90.3% for anomalous behaviors, reduces portfolio volatility by 32.1%, and decreases maximum drawdown by 41.5% compared to unregulated markets. The framework operationalizes the "Agentic Regulator" paradigm through practical implementation on resource-constrained environments (Google Colab), demonstrating that autonomous regulatory agents can effectively quarantine malicious trading entities while preserving market innovation. Our ablation study confirms the critical contribution of each regulatory component-behavioral anomaly detection, collusion monitoring, market stability assessment, and LLM-based reasoning-to overall governance effectiveness. This research provides the first empirical validation of agentic regulatory architectures for real-time financial market governance.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous, agentic AI systems are beginning to make real-time pricing and inventory decisions across hospitality revenue management without a standardized, machine-readable governance layer to keep those decisions economically bounded once human review is removed. The governance logic is tested through a 10,000-iteration stochastic simulation comparing an AKIF-governed agent against an unaligned, volume-maximising AI agent and a legacy human-operated revenue management system. The governed agent achieves consistently superior gross operating profit under simulated demand shocks and materially less long-term rate erosion than the unaligned agent, while exposing a case in which conventional RevPAR reporting would have rewarded the unaligned agent's value-destroying behaviour. records.title: The Wheel of Intelligence: Contract-Enforced Closed-Loop Architectures for Reliable LLM-Agent Systems
records.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that retrieve documents, maintain state, and execute tools, yet open-loop execution makes failures hard to audit and unsafe actions hard to prevent. We introduce the Wheel of Intelligence (WoI), a contract-enforced closed-loop architecture that separates a proposer policy from a Self-Reflection verifier gate (V SR). WoI represents intermediate artifacts as typed knowledge objects with explicit provenance, supporting deterministic checks for citation validity and tool-safety policies, and optional semantic verification via a separate entailment judge. We formalize systemlevel metrics that capture reliability and cost, including Loop Cost (LC), Audit Rejection Rate (ARR), Integration Success Rate (ISR), and Catastrophic Action Rate (CAR), alongside evidencebased measures of claim support. We provide a reproducible evaluation harness for multi-hop question answering with retrieval and for a sandboxed file-tool environment, enabling controlled measurement of the verification-latency trade-off as verifier strength increases.</jats:p>

records.title: Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model
records.abstract: Abstract Tabular data, spreadsheets organized in rows and columns, are ubiquitous across scientific fields, from biomedicine to particle physics to economics and climate science 1,2 . The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has great potential to reshape the landscape of combating misinformation. Generally, LLMs can be a double‐edged sword in the fight. On the one hand, LLMs bring promising opportunities for combating misinformation due to their profound world knowledge and strong reasoning abilities. Thus, one emerging question is: can we utilize LLMs to combat misinformation? On the other hand, the critical challenge is that LLMs can be easily leveraged to generate deceptive misinformation at scale. In this paper, we first systematically review the history of combating misinformation before the advent of LLMs. Then we illustrate the current efforts and present an outlook for these two fundamental questions, respectively. The goal of this survey paper is to facilitate the progress of utilizing LLMs for fighting misinformation and call for interdisciplinary efforts from different stakeholders for combating LLM‐generated misinformation.

records.title: ProSA: Assessing and Understanding the Prompt Sensitivity of LLMs
records.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, but their performance is highly sensitive to the prompts utilized. This variability poses challenges for accurate assessment and user satisfaction. Current research frequently overlooks instance-level prompt variations and their implications on subjective evaluations. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ProSA, a framework designed to evaluate and comprehend prompt sensitivity in LLMs. ProSA incorporates a novel sensitivity metric, PromptSensiScore, and leverages decoding confidence to elucidate underlying mechanisms. Our extensive study, spanning multiple tasks, uncovers that prompt sensitivity fluctuates across datasets and models, with larger models exhibiting enhanced robustness. We observe that few-shot examples can alleviate this sensitivity issue, and subjective evaluations are also susceptible to prompt sensitivities, particularly in complex, reasoning-oriented tasks. Furthermore, our findings indicate that higher model confidence correlates with increased prompt robustness. We believe this work will serve as a helpful tool in studying prompt sensitivity of LLMs. The project is released at: https://github.com/open-compass/ProSA .

records.title: On Catastrophic Inheritance of Large Foundation Models
records.abstract: Large foundation models (LFMs) are claiming incredible performances. records.title: The Vulnerability of Language Model Benchmarks: Do They Accurately Reflect True LLM Performance?
records.abstract: The pursuit of leaderboard rankings in Large Language Models (LLMs) has created a fundamental paradox: models excel at standardized tests while failing to demonstrate genuine language understanding and adaptability. Our systematic analysis of NLP evaluation frameworks reveals pervasive vulnerabilities across the evaluation spectrum, from basic metrics to complex benchmarks like GLUE and MMLU. These vulnerabilities manifest through benchmark exploitation, dataset contamination, and evaluation bias, creating a false perception of progress in language understanding capabilities. Through extensive review of contemporary evaluation approaches, we identify significant limitations in static benchmark designs, human evaluation protocols, and LLM-as-judge frameworks, all of which compromise the reliability of current performance assessments. As LLM capabilities evolve and existing benchmarks become redundant, we lay the groundwork for new evaluation methods that resist manipulation, minimize data contamination, and assess domain-specific tasks. This requires frameworks that are adapted dynamically, addressing current limitations and providing a more accurate reflection of LLM performance.

records.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
records.abstract: Language models are increasingly being deployed for general problem solving across a wide range of tasks, but are still confined to token-level, left-to-right decision-making processes during inference. This means they can fall short in tasks that require exploration, strategic lookahead, or where initial decisions play a pivotal role. To surmount these challenges, we introduce a new framework for language model inference, Tree of Thoughts (ToT), which generalizes over the popular Chain of Thought approach to prompting language models, and enables exploration over coherent units of text (thoughts) that serve as intermediate steps toward problem solving. ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices. Our experiments show that ToT significantly enhances language models' problem-solving abilities on three novel tasks requiring non-trivial planning or search: Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords. For instance, in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%. Code repo with all prompts: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm.
